opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we think about a lot, and I'd say a few things.

First, I'd push back a little on the idea that browser use is close to being commoditized. Getting an agent to click around a website in a demo is one thing. Getting it to complete a task reliably, on the messy long tail of real websites, with pop-ups, logins, dynamic content, and sites that change week to week, is a very different bar. There's still a big gap between "it works sometimes" and "it works well enough that you'd trust it to run in the background without watching it." A lot of our post-training effort goes into closing that gap.

Second, and more fundamentally, we don't see browser use as the product. It's a capability in service of the product. What we care about is the end-to-end experience for the user: an assistant that monitors the web for you, takes actions on your behalf, and comes back with something useful. For that, we're post-training for the specific distribution of tasks our users care about, the specific failure modes we see in production, and the specific behaviors we want, like knowing when to stop, when to ask for clarification, and how to report back. A general-purpose model trained to be decent at everything won't automatically be optimized for that.

Third, there's a data flywheel. Because we're deployed, we see real tasks and real failures, and that tells us exactly where to focus. That feedback loop is hard to replicate if you're building a general model that has to serve every use case at once.

And finally, we're pragmatic. If the frontier general-purpose models get really good at browser use, that's great for us. We'll build on top of them, and our post-training starts from a stronger base. The value isn't in owning a capability that everyone else lacks forever. It's in being the team that turns these capabilities into something people actually rely on day to day. That means constantly re-evaluating where our own training adds value and where it's better to just use what's out there.

So I'd frame it less as "will our model stay better at browsing" and more as "are we building the best product for proactive, web-based assistance," with post-training as one of the tools we use to get there.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training targets users’ specific task distribution and production failure modes to make browser tasks reliable enough to trust.

r002.rationale: It describes improving reliability on messy websites, but does not state that post-training extends workflow complexity beyond what foundation models support out of the box.

r003.rationale: The response discusses building on stronger general-purpose models, but does not mention lower costs than routing requests to external model APIs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, honestly, because it's the obvious question anyone would ask about what we're doing. If the frontier labs are shipping computer-use and browser-use agents, and open-weight models are catching up on the basic "click this, type that, navigate here" loop, what's the point of post-training your own model for it?

I'd break it down a few ways. The first is that "general-purpose browser use" is a bit of a misnomer. The benchmarks measure something like, can the model complete a task on a reasonably well-behaved website when given a clean instruction. And yes, that's getting commoditized, and it should. That's great. But the long tail of what you hit in the real world is enormous. Sites that are adversarial, sites that are broken in weird ways, flows that require persistent state across dozens of steps, tasks where the right thing to do is stop and not take an action. The gap between "works on the demo" and "works at scale with real reliability" is where almost all the value is, and that gap doesn't close just because the base capability is widely available.

The second thing is that post-training is not really about teaching the model to use a browser. The base models already know how to use a browser, more or less. What you're actually doing in post-training is shaping the behavior to match your distribution of tasks, your error tolerance, your latency budget, and your definition of what a good trajectory looks like. That's specific to what you're building. Even if I had access to the very best general model, I'd still want to do that shaping, because a generalist model is optimized for an average over use cases that aren't mine.

And then the third piece is data and feedback loops. If you're running an agent in production, you're generating trajectories, successes, failures, places where a human had to step in. That's a proprietary signal that no one else has, and post-training is the mechanism for feeding it back into the model. So the value of the post-training compounds over time in a way that just consuming someone else's API doesn't. Your model gets better at your problems specifically.

Now, I want to be honest about the other side of it. There's a real risk of over-investing in capabilities that will be free in twelve months. We've all seen teams build elaborate scaffolding around a limitation that a model release just erased. So the discipline I try to keep is to ask, for any given thing we're training in, is this something that's fundamentally about our task distribution and our data, or is it a general capability that's just not quite there yet? If it's the latter, you should probably wait, or build the thinnest possible bridge and expect to rip it out. If it's the former, that's durable, and that's where you lean in.

So I guess the short answer is, the browser-use part gets commoditized, and I'm happy about that. The part that doesn't get commoditized is knowing what your agent should actually do, reliably, in your environment, and having the loop that keeps improving it. That's where the post-training lives, and I think that stays valuable for a long time.

r001.rationale: It says post-training shapes behavior for the product’s task distribution and error tolerance, improving reliability on its specific problems.

r002.rationale: It describes complex workflows and long-tail cases, but does not clearly state that post-training extends workflow complexity beyond what foundation models support out of the box.

r003.rationale: It discusses proprietary feedback and the limits of relying on someone else’s API, but does not state that serving its own model costs less.

astra-6.text:
I think the question is where the value moves as that baseline capability gets better. If everyone has access to a model that can navigate a website, click buttons, and fill out forms, then those actions themselves become less of a differentiator.

But there’s still a gap between being able to use a browser and reliably accomplishing what someone actually wants. Can the model handle a long workflow, recover when something unexpected happens, and recognize when it needs to ask for clarification? That’s where I think post-training can continue to matter: shaping the behavior around the task, rather than just improving individual browser actions.

And I wouldn’t assume that a particular advantage from post-training lasts forever. You have to keep evaluating against the improving general-purpose models. If they solve a piece of the problem well enough, you build on that and focus your effort on the failures that still matter to users.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training can help a model reliably complete user tasks, but does not clearly tie that improvement to a product’s specific use cases.

r002.rationale: It identifies long workflows as an area where post-training may matter, but does not state that post-training extends workflow complexity beyond what foundation models support out of the box.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about serving costs or comparison with external model API providers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value shifts. If the underlying ability to navigate a website and click the right buttons becomes broadly available, then that capability alone becomes less of a differentiator. But there’s still a gap between being able to use a browser and reliably completing something useful for a person.

A lot of that comes down to understanding the user’s intent, handling ambiguity, recognizing when something has gone wrong, and knowing when to ask for help. And then there’s the question of whether you can do that consistently across long workflows, where a small mistake early on can affect everything downstream.

So I’d think of post-training as an ongoing process, rather than a one-time asset. The value is in the feedback loop: understanding where the model fails in actual use, getting the right signals, and improving the behavior. As general capabilities improve, you should absolutely take advantage of that. But the bar for what users expect also goes up. The question becomes less, ‘Can it operate the browser?’ and more, ‘Can I trust it to get this task done?’

r001.rationale: It says post-training improves behavior based on failures in actual use and emphasizes reliably completing useful tasks, communicating improved reliability for the product’s use cases.

r002.rationale: It mentions consistency across long workflows, but does not say post-training extends workflow complexity beyond what foundation models support out of the box.

r003.rationale: It does not mention serving costs or compare an in-house browser-use model with external model API providers.
